result: {"decisions":[{"point":"D2","problem":"How to establish that a model believes a statement is false so that its output can be labeled a lie rather than a mistake.","did":"They operationalized beliefs through consistent responses in neutral contexts without pressure to lie, and used this to label on-policy outputs.","alternatives_named":["off-policy false statements","a common-sense notion of lying requiring belief awareness during the lie"],"stated_reason":"Deceptive intent is hard to verify in LLMs, so a measurable non-deceptionist, assertion-based definition strikes a balance between usefulness and measurability.","quote":"We operationalize beliefs following the approach of Ren et al. (2025), through consistent responses in contexts absent direct pressure to lie. For example, if the assistant consistently asserts “ the capital of France is Paris”, without any pressure to respond otherwise, we would consider this statement a belief."},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether harm-pressure contradictions of established beliefs are real lies or just random sampling noise from uncertain models.","did":"They measured a baseline contradiction rate on a held-out neutral template and kept only harmful templates whose contradiction rate was at least four times higher.","alternatives_named":["keeping all harmful templates"],"stated_reason":"This ensures contradictions are unlikely to be chance and are instead deliberately false responses triggered by the harmful intent.","quote":"For each template, we again measure contradiction frequency and retain only those harmful templates whose contradiction rate is at least four times higher than in the neutral validation case."},{"point":"D3","problem":"Whether to accept HP-C labels where the model's established belief is factually incorrect, including cases where the 'lie' is the correct answer.","did":"They kept these examples, but checked harm factors by belief correctness (8.1 vs 3.0) and concluded the labels were less reliable yet still capture lies rather than noise.","alternatives_named":["discarding examples with incorrect beliefs"],"stated_reason":"Correct lies test whether detectors work when factual correctness cannot serve as a proxy, and a harm factor of 3.0 is well above the 1.0 expected from chance.","quote":"We conclude that the labels in HP-C for questions where the assistant has an incorrect belief are less reliable than when the belief is correct, but we are confident that they capture lies rather than noise."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to prevent detectors from exploiting dataset artifacts such as explicit lie instructions in system prompts.","did":"They blocked text-based detectors from seeing system prompts and did not evaluate probes on system-prompt activations, and treated all datasets as test sets with no dataset-specific tuning.","alternatives_named":["giving detectors full access to system prompts"],"stated_reason":"The lie instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset that would let text-based detectors reliably detect lies.","quote":"As these instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset, we prevent such detectors from directly accessing system prompts. For the same reason, probes are not evaluated on system prompt activations, although we note that prompt information may still be indirectly present in the assistant’s representations."},{"point":"D2","problem":"How to set decision thresholds and aggregate performance so detectors are compared fairly and realistically.","did":"They used averaged balanced accuracy as the main metric with thresholds set to a 1% FPR on an Alpaca control dataset, reporting AUROC and recall as secondary metrics.","alternatives_named":["recall alone"],"stated_reason":"Balanced accuracy penalizes detectors that merely trigger on deception-related contexts and accounts for class imbalance, while the Alpaca FPR constraint reflects monitoring needs.","quote":"Unlike recall, balanced accuracy ensures that performance is fairly assessed across lies and honest cases of our datasets. This is essential for the use cases alignment evaluations, where the reliability of a model’s self-reports is under scrutiny"},{"point":"D1","problem":"How to test that fine-tuned backdoor lying reflects a learned concept rather than shallow token matching.","did":"They generated the Soft-Trigger dataset using triggers unseen during training but belonging to the same category as the training triggers.","alternatives_named":["using the exact trigger tokens seen in training"],"stated_reason":"To reduce the chance that the dataset captures shallow token-matching instead of learned lying.","quote":"That is, we generate the dataset with triggers unseen during training, but belonging to the same category, to reduce the chance we are capturing shallow token-matching instead of learned lying."},{"point":"D5","problem":"Why LLM-as-a-Judge performed unexpectedly poorly on HP-C, and whether label noise from incorrect beliefs was responsible.","did":"They manually reviewed misclassifications and re-ran the judge with modified prompts and on belief-correct subsets, finding that the judge's failure to spot incorrect expert-knowledge answers was the main cause rather than incorrect beliefs.","alternatives_named":["incorrect beliefs in the labels as the main cause"],"stated_reason":"AUROC only rose to 0.76 when restricted to correct beliefs, but rose to 0.82 when the judge scored incorrectness instead of lying.","quote":"However, as the AUROC merely increased to 0.76 (+0.03), we do not see it as the main cause for its weak results."},{"point":"D6","problem":"How strongly to interpret the LLM-as-a-Judge's strong average performance as evidence for the method.","did":"They cautioned against reading the results as an endorsement of relying solely on LLM judges, since the judge fails on lies that depend on private knowledge and fact-checking.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"The HP-KR truthfulness hinges on the assistant's actual knowledge, which is hard for an external judge to infer, and future judges may not fact-check reliably.","quote":"Overall, we caution against interpreting these results as an endorsement for solely relying on approaches like LLM-as-a-Judge to detect sophisticated lies by future models, especially when the judge model cannot be expected to perform reliable fact-checking."},{"point":"D5","problem":"How to explain Self-Evaluation's varying performance across datasets, and whether its success reflects detection or confession.","did":"They interpreted its performance as depending on the model's inclination to disobey lie instructions or break character, supported by an experiment framing the statement as coming from another model.","alternatives_named":[],"stated_reason":"Performance was best where models were merely encouraged to lie and near chance where lying was inherent or fine-tuned, and improved when the statement was attributed to another model.","quote":"Overall, we interpret that the effectiveness of self-evaluation depends on the model’s inclination to disobey lie-inducing instructions, break character during role-play, or in the case of GS, contradict the intended behavior from evaluation testbed rather than to maximize detector performance.","quote":"Finally, our reported methods are baselines that we have not optimized, since our goal was to provide an evaluation testbed
